sections.title: Memory beyond the prompt
paragraphs: Imagine an open-book exam. You cannot memorize every page of the textbook, but you can bring an indexed notebook and look up what you need when a question arrives. Large language models work the same way at scale: they reason well, but they cannot fit your entire company wiki inside one request.

Every turn has a fixed {{contextWindow}} — a maximum amount of text the {{model}} can read at once. Paste in too much and you must cut, summarize, or drop facts. That limit is short-term working space, not a permanent filing cabinet.

{{semanticMemory}} is the durable store outside that window: policy PDFs, support FAQs, rubric docs, API references. At query time you {{retrieval}} the few passages that matter and place them in the prompt. The {{model}} still generates the answer — but from evidence you chose.

Training {{weights}} teach broad language patterns, not a reliable record of every internal fact. A {{model}} may sound confident about your refund policy while inventing details it never saw. For company-specific truth, external memory beats hoping the weights remembered.

In AiEval you will compare {{model}} answers about internal documents the {{model}} was never trained on. That only works when you can fetch the right source text first — another reason {{semanticMemory}} matters before you judge quality.
You already saw how {{judge}} automation needs parseable output; retrieval is the next pipeline leg — fetching evidence before generation.
bullets: {{contextWindow}} — how much fits in one request.
{{semanticMemory}} — indexed knowledge searched at query time.
{{retrieval}} — pull relevant passages into the prompt before answering.

check.prompt: Your team has a 200-page employee handbook. A colleague wants to paste the entire PDF into every system prompt "so the {{model}} always knows the rules." What is the better approach?
check.answer: Index handbook chunks in a vector store and retrieve relevant passages per question
choices: Paste the full PDF into every system prompt
Index handbook chunks in a vector store and retrieve relevant passages per question
Fine-tune the model weekly on the whole handbook
Ask users to quote page numbers in every message
check.explanation: The {{contextWindow}} cannot hold a full handbook on every turn, and bloated prompts waste tokens. Split the doc into {{chunk}}s, store {{embedding}}s, and use {{retrieval}} so only relevant passages enter the prompt.

sections.title: Search by meaning
paragraphs: Keyword search fails when users paraphrase. A customer asks to "recover account access" while your FAQ title says "password reset." Ctrl+F misses the match even though the meaning is the same.

{{semanticMemory}} pipelines split source documents into {{chunk}}s — short passages small enough to rank and fit in context. Each {{chunk}} becomes an {{embedding}}: numbers that capture meaning, not just spelling.

At query time the question is embedded too. {{retrieval}} compares the query {{embedding}} to stored {{chunk}} {{embedding}}s and returns the closest matches. Similar meaning lands nearby even when words differ.
Click each scenario below to see what {{retrieval}} should surface. Notice how the best {{chunk}} is about intent, not exact keyword overlap.
This is the core idea behind semantic search and RAG: find the right evidence first, then let the {{model}} write an answer grounded in what you retrieved.

reveals.prompt: User asks: "How do I get back into my account?" — which store entry should rank highest?
reveals.reveal: FAQ: "Reset your password from the sign-in page" — paraphrased intent matches even without the word "account."

reveals.prompt: Evaluator asks: "What makes a strong rubric row?" — which doc chunk helps?
reveals.reveal: Rubric guide: "Each criterion needs a clear anchor for score 1 vs score 5" — matches evaluation wording, not the word "row."

reveals.prompt: Developer asks: "How do I list evaluations via API?" — which chunk fits?
reveals.reveal: API reference: "GET /api/evaluations returns all saved evaluations" — technical paraphrase still maps to the endpoint description.

check.prompt: Support tickets use varied wording: "locked out," "forgot login," "can't sign in." Your FAQ uses "password reset." Which lookup strategy fits best?
choices: Exact keyword match on "password reset" only
Sort FAQs alphabetically and show the first ten
Ask the user to rephrase until keywords match
check.explanation: {{retrieval}} with {{embedding}}s matches meaning across phrasing. Keyword-only search misses paraphrases that humans treat as the same question.

sections.title: From memory to hands-on search
paragraphs: Production {{semanticMemory}} rarely stops at pure vector search. Teams combine semantic scores with keyword filters, metadata tags (team, product, date), and re-ranking before anything reaches the {{contextWindow}}.

Teaching shortcut: the next lab uses **2D** {{embedding}}s so you can see closeness on a map. Real systems use hundreds or thousands of dimensions — the idea is the same, only the geometry is harder to draw.
Try the optional **Semantic memory practice** lab from the sidebar for a quick ranking drill. The **Semantic search lab** on the track goes deeper with a 2D map.
In the **Semantic search lab** you will type queries, watch similarity scores, and see which {{chunk}}s rank highest. That is {{retrieval}} without API keys — the same ranking step RAG depends on.
After that, the **RAG playground** assembles retrieved {{chunk}}s into a prompt and previews a stub answer. You will see how {{semanticMemory}} feeds generation, not replaces it.
When you run evaluations in AiEval, ask whether the winning answer used the right retrieved evidence — not just fluent prose. Good {{retrieval}} is often the difference between grounded and guessed.
bullets: Real stacks: hybrid search, metadata filters, re-ranking.
Next: Semantic search lab — rank {{chunk}}s in 2D.
Then: RAG playground — context assembly + stub answer.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: what is {{semanticMemory}} in an LLM app?
accept: knowledge outside the prompt retrieved by meaning
facts stored outside the model retrieved by meaning
check.explanation: {{semanticMemory}} keeps durable facts outside the {{contextWindow}}. {{retrieval}} fetches the right {{chunk}}s by meaning so the {{model}} answers from evidence you control.

recapQuestions.prompt: Why is pasting a full company wiki into every prompt a weak {{semanticMemory}} strategy?
recapQuestions.answer: It exceeds the context window and buries the relevant facts
choices: Models cannot read PDFs at all
It exceeds the context window and buries the relevant facts
Retrieval works only on training data
recapQuestions.explanation: The {{contextWindow}} is finite. Dumping everything wastes space and makes it harder to surface the few {{chunk}}s that matter. Indexed {{retrieval}} keeps prompts focused.

recapQuestions.prompt: What are the three main steps from source doc to answer in a typical RAG-style system?
recapQuestions.answer: Chunk documents, retrieve relevant chunks, generate an answer
choices: Chunk documents, retrieve relevant chunks, generate an answer
Copy Wikipedia, paste prompt, score with a rubric
Memorize the test set, fine-tune, skip retrieval
recapQuestions.explanation: Split docs into {{chunk}}s, use {{embedding}}s for {{retrieval}}, then let the {{model}} generate using what you fetched. That is {{semanticMemory}} feeding the {{contextWindow}} on demand.
